meta.title: Maths Map - Level 1 Item Bank (Draft for parent review)
meta.curriculumSource: Victorian Curriculum F-10 (2.0) Mathematics, Level 1. Codes are © VCAA, CC-BY-NC 3.0.

scoring.notes: choice/order items: correct = 2, otherwise 0. observe items: parent uses rubric to award 0/1/2.

itemTypes.order: Child taps items into the correct sequence
itemTypes.observe: Parent-led task with household materials; parent ticks secure / partial / not yet using the rubric

items.prompt: What number comes right after 59?
Tap the numbers from smallest to biggest:
Which number is BIGGER: 46 or 64?
35 is the same as…
Counting to 120 by tens
items.observeScript: Put out about 50 buttons, pasta pieces or coins. Say: 'Count these by making piles of 10, and tell me how many there are altogether.' Then ask: 'What number comes after 119?' Watch HOW they count — one-by-one, or grouping into tens?

observeRubric.secure: Groups into tens, skip counts (10, 20, 30…) and says the total, and knows 120 follows 119
observeRubric.partial: Counts correctly but one-by-one, or skip counts with small slips and needs reminding
observeRubric.notYet: Loses track, miscounts through a group, or cannot keep going past about 30 without a lot of help

items.prompt: 8 is made from 5 and…
24 is the same as 10 + ?
Which one shows 35 split into tens and ones?
7 and what makes 10?
Partitioning one number in different ways
items.observeScript: Give your child 13 counters (buttons, pasta, LEGO). Say: 'Show me 13 with these. Now show me 13 a DIFFERENT way — like moving some into a group of 10.' Ask for at least two different partitions, e.g. 10+3, 5+5+3, 8+5.

observeRubric.secure: Shows 2+ partitions including a tens-and-ones split (10 and 3)
observeRubric.partial: Finds one or two partitions but needs prompting, or only splits into small parts (e.g. 6+7) without using 10
observeRubric.notYet: Cannot reliably partition, or loses track of how many there are

items.prompt: Count by 2s: 2, 4, 6, 8, …
Count by 5s: 5, 10, 15, …
Sam counts 47 marbles by making groups of 10. The last group has 7 in it. How many FULL groups of 10 does he have?
Counting a large collection by tens
items.observeScript: Put out about 40 small objects (buttons, pasta, coins). Say: 'Count these by making groups of 10. How many are there?' You can stack $1 coins in piles of 10 if you have them. Watch the strategy, not just the answer.

observeRubric.secure: Groups in 10s (even roughly) and skip counts to arrive at the total
observeRubric.partial: Groups in tens but skip counts unreliably, or recounts one-by-one afterwards to check
observeRubric.notYet: Cannot keep count beyond a small set, or loses the groups

items.prompt: 8 + 5 = ?  (Hint: 8 + 2 = 10, then a bit more…)
Solving story problems and explaining the strategy
items.observeScript: Ask these two out loud, one at a time: 'You had 9 grapes. You ate 4. How many are left?' and 'You had 7 grapes. Gran gave you 8 more. How many now?' Then ask: 'HOW did you work it out?' Listen for a strategy (counting on, part-part-whole, making 10), not just the answer.

observeRubric.secure: Solves both and can explain a strategy (counting on/back, making 10, part-part-whole)
observeRubric.partial: Solves both with fingers or counting materials, but can't yet explain the strategy; or solves one fluently
observeRubric.notYet: Cannot solve either, or guesses without a counting method

items.prompt: You buy a toy car for $8 and pay with a $10 note. How much change do you get?
There are 6 people on the bus. 4 more get on. How many people are on the bus now?
You had $10. You spent $4 on a snack. How much money is left?
Play shop with real or pretend money
items.observeScript: Set up a pretend shop: price 3–4 items $1–$10, give your child $15 of play money (or real $1/$2 coins). Ask them to buy TWO items, say how much they spent, and how much they have left. Then reverse: 'What if they wanted to buy the $7 toy — could they afford it?'

observeRubric.secure: Chooses items within budget, adds costs, works out change or left-over amount with minimal prompting
observeRubric.partial: Completes purchase with lots of prompting, or needs you to do the adding
observeRubric.notYet: Cannot combine prices or reason about having enough/not enough, even with prompting

items.prompt: There are 3 cars and each car has 4 wheels. How many wheels in total?
Share 10 biscuits equally between 2 friends. How many biscuits does each friend get?
You have 12 apples. You pack them into bags of 4. How many bags do you fill?
Share 8 coins equally between 4 people. How many coins does each person get?
Equal sharing with leftovers
items.observeScript: Give 14 counters. Say: 'Share these equally between 2 plates — one for you, one for me.' Then: 'Now share 15 counters equally between the 3 of us (you, me, a toy).' Watch whether they deal one at a time, and whether they notice any leftovers in the second round.

observeRubric.secure: Shares 14 between 2 evenly AND notices 15 between 3 leaves a leftover (or shares 15 as 5 each if using all)
observeRubric.partial: Shares the 14 evenly; needs help or prompts to notice the leftover with 15 between 3

items.prompt: What comes next? 2, 4, 6, 8, …
What comes next? 5, 10, 15, …
What comes next? 10, 20, 30, …
When you count by 2s starting from 0, the last digit of every number is…
Building a skip-count pattern
items.observeScript: Give your child blocks, shells or coins. Say: 'Make a row showing 2, then 4, then 6, then 8 — show me what comes next.' Then: 'Count with me by 10s to 100.' Watch whether the pattern matches the counting.

observeRubric.secure: Extends the 2-4-6-8 pattern correctly and skip counts in 2s, 5s or 10s aloud to 100
observeRubric.partial: Extends the pattern with prompts, or skip counts with occasional slips
observeRubric.notYet: Cannot extend the pattern or skip count without full support

items.prompt: 🔴 🔵 🔴 🔵 🔴 … what comes next?
Find the repeating unit in: ✦✦★ ✦✦★ ✦✦★
One number doesn't belong: 2, 4, 6, 9, 10. Which one?
Pattern: ★◆◆★◆◆★◆◆. What are the next two?
Making and continuing a repeating pattern
items.observeScript: Give beads, blocks, buttons or fruit-loop cereal in 2 colours. Make this pattern and ask your child to CONTINUE it: red, blue, blue, red, blue, blue… Then ask: 'What is the repeating part? How many of each colour would the pattern need for the first 9 pieces?'

observeRubric.secure: Continues the pattern correctly AND names the repeating unit (red-blue-blue)
observeRubric.partial: Continues the pattern but cannot explain or name the unit

items.prompt: Which holds more water: a bathtub or a cup?
Which is heavier: a bag of rice or a feather?
Which takes longer: a blink or a nap?
Two strings were measured with paperclips. String A is 8 paperclips long. String B is 5 paperclips long. Which string is longer?
Ordering by length, mass, capacity
items.observeScript: Round 1 (length): Find 3 things to place in order of length (spoon, pencil, book) — ask your child to order them and explain how they decided (compare directly or use string). Round 2 (capacity): Compare 3 containers (cup, bowl, jug) by pouring — which holds most? Round 3 (mass): Hold a book vs a feather — 'which is heavier? How do you know?'

observeRubric.secure: Orders in all three rounds and explains HOW (direct comparison, pouring, hefting) using comparing words (longer, heavier, holds more)
observeRubric.partial: Gets 1–2 rounds right, may need prompts or guess
observeRubric.notYet: Cannot compare or order even with direct side-by-side or pouring

items.prompt: Mia measured the desk with icy-pole sticks laid end to end. Sam measured the same desk with pencils. Why did they get different numbers?
True or false: when you measure, you can leave GAPS between the units.
Which is longer: 9 paperclips or 6 paperclips?
Why should we use the SAME size units when we measure?
options: So different people's results can be compared

items.prompt: Measuring the table with informal units
items.observeScript: Ask your child to measure the width of the dining table (or a shelf) using toy cars, shoes or building blocks laid end-to-end. They count the units aloud. Then ask: 'What would happen to the number if you left gaps? Why?'

observeRubric.secure: Lays units end-to-end without gaps/overlaps, counts accurately, and explains gaps would give the wrong (bigger) answer
observeRubric.partial: Measures but leaves some gaps/overlaps or miscounts by a little
observeRubric.notYet: Cannot lay units end-to-end or count them

items.prompt: Which is the shortest amount of time?
Put in order: afternoon, morning, night
Put these months in order: April, January, August
How many days are in one week?
Sequencing events and knowing time words
items.observeScript: Ask: 'What day comes after Tuesday?' 'What month comes after December?' 'Put these in order: breakfast, lunch, dinner.' 'Is a movie closer to an hour, a day or a week?' 'Is a school term closer to a week, a month or a year?'

observeRubric.secure: Answers all correctly — days of week, months, sequencing meals, and sensible hour/day comparisons
observeRubric.partial: Days and meal sequencing fine; months or time-scale comparisons shaky
observeRubric.notYet: Cannot sequence even the meal routine, or mixes up days/months entirely

items.prompt: Which shape has exactly 3 sides?
Which one of these is round? 🔺  🟦  ⚫
How many corners does a square have?
Which one doesn't belong: circle, oval, triangle?
Sorting a bag of shapes and explaining the rule
items.observeScript: Cut out or gather 10+ shapes: circles, ovals, triangles, squares, rectangles (any sizes), plus 3-D objects if you have them (blocks, ball, tin). Ask: 'Sort these into TWO groups.' Ask: 'What is your rule? How are the shapes in a group the same, and how are the two groups different?' Then: 'Find a circle, a triangle and a rectangle in this room.'

observeRubric.secure: Sorts into sensible groups AND states a rule in terms of features (round/straight sides, number of sides/corners); finds matching objects in the room
observeRubric.partial: Sorts by eye but struggles to state a rule, or matches only the obvious shapes
observeRubric.notYet: Cannot sort meaningfully or find shapes in the environment

items.prompt: A robot needs to go forward, forward, turn right, forward. Which command fits?
Which word means moving in REVERSE?
'Left' and 'right' are words about…
Follow the directions: 'three steps forward, then one step back'. Where do you end up, compared to the start?
Being a robot and giving directions
items.observeScript: Part A (you are the robot): Your child gives YOU directions from the doorway to the kitchen table using only words like 'forward, back, left, right, turn around'. You must only do exactly what they say. Part B (they are the robot): You give them a 4-step route around the lounge room and they follow it. Note how precise the language is.

observeRubric.secure: Both parts work — gives unambiguous multi-step directions and follows yours using left/right/forward/back
observeRubric.partial: One direction works; left/right still mixed up or steps vague ('go there')
observeRubric.notYet: Cannot follow simple directions or give any in order

items.prompt: Which question is BEST for collecting data by asking people?
Tally marks are drawn in groups of…
Count the tally marks: |||| |||  — how many?
Which makes counting results easiest?
options: a long list in the order people answered

items.prompt: Survey the family and tally the results
items.observeScript: Ask your child to do a mini-survey of the household: favourite ice-cream flavour (give 3 choices: chocolate, vanilla, strawberry). They prepare a piece of paper with the three flavours, ask each person, and record with tally marks. Then count up each group. You can check their totals together.

observeRubric.secure: Sets up categories, tallies accurately (groups of 5), and counts the totals correctly
observeRubric.partial: Tallies but miscounts, or needs categories set up for them
observeRubric.notYet: Cannot manage a tally recording — needs the process modelled step by step

items.prompt: One smiley 😊 = one vote. 😊😊😊😊😊 votes for apples. How many votes for apples?
Votes: apples 😊😊😊, bananas 😊😊😊😊😊. Which did more children choose?
Count by fives to find the total of two full tallies: 5, 10, …
Nobody chose pears. How should the pear column look in the display?
Making a one-to-one display and comparing
items.observeScript: Using the ice-cream survey from before (or a fresh sort of 20 buttons by colour), help your child make a one-to-one picture display: one sticker/drawing per vote, grouped by category in columns. Then ask: 'Which was most popular? How many more chose X than Y?' Let them count by fives in the columns.

observeRubric.secure: Builds a tidy one-to-one display, identifies most/least popular, and works out the difference by counting
observeRubric.partial: Builds the display but comparing/difference needs support
observeRubric.notYet: Cannot organise a one-to-one display at all
